chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from 'Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him, 'Does a man lead his family in the prayer of the two Eids on the roof or in a house?' He said, 'He does not lead them, nor do they go out, and there is no obligation upon the women to go out.' And he said, 'Reduce their formality/dress so that they do not ask to go out.'
And Isma'il ibn Jabir narrated from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him, 'What did you see regarding the prayer of the two Eids, is there an Adhan and Iqamah in them?' He said, 'There is no Adhan and no Iqamah in them, but the call is made: "As-Salat, As-Salat" three times. And there is no pulpit (minbar) in them; the pulpit is not moved from its place, but something resembling a pulpit is made for the Imam from clay, so he stands upon it and addresses the people, then he descends.'

key_terms.إِقَامَةٌ: Iqamah (second call to prayer, immediately preceding the prayer)
key_terms.صَلَاةُ الْعِيدَيْنِ: The two Eid prayers (Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on Adhan, Iqamah, and women's attendance for Eid prayers in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In the Shia jurisprudential tradition, the Eid prayer is distinguished by the absence of formal Adhan and Iqamah, relying instead on a simple triple call of 'As-Salat', reflecting its status as a communal gathering rather than a formal congregational prayer with a fixed pulpit. The Imam utilizes a temporary clay structure for the sermon, emphasizing the transient nature of the venue, while the ruling that women are not obligated to attend underscores the principle of 'Iqallu la-hunna' (reducing their adornment) to minimize their desire to go out, thereby preserving modesty and ease.
